chunk_findings.detail:
`hide`, `next`, `tasks` and `show_hidden` are roadmap-only options — the knob doc spells this out ("the roadmap also takes hide … next … tasks … show_hidden"), and the intent lists them as `[export.roadmap]` settings. But the change puts them in the single global `EXPORT_TABLE_KEYS` frozenset and validates them for *every* `[export.<doc>]` table via `_roadmap_keys_problem(doc, t)`. So with a config such as

    [export.changelog]
    hide = ["BL-"]
    next = 3

the table is now considered valid (no "unknown key" warning, which the same `tables` doc promises for keys a doc does not understand) even though only the roadmap reads these values — the changelog export silently ignores them, and the user gets no signal that the option had no effect. Conversely a typo in an unrelated doc's table can now produce a roadmap-specific message (`[export.changelog].next must be an integer >= 0`) for a key that document does not support. Either the keys need to be checked per document (`_roadmap_keys_problem` only when `doc == "roadmap"`, with the keys kept out of the global set or filtered back out for other docs), or the accepted-key set has to stay doc-agnostic and the doc text corrected.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/export.py:98 (EXPORT_TABLE_KEYS) and :115 (_roadmap_keys_problem)

chunk_findings.detail: `owner` maps every task of a phase back to that phase (`owner[t.id] = pid`), and `before(pid)` unions the unmet deps of the phase *and of all its tasks* without ever excluding `pid` itself. So whenever one task of a phase waits on another still-open task of the same phase, the returned set contains the phase itself: phase `P1` with open tasks `T1`/`T2` where `T1` waits on `T2` yields `before("P1") == {"P1"}` — a self-edge. That graph is passed straight to `RC.order(by_id, _phase_before(...), key)`. A phase with ordered tasks (write → review, both open) is common input, and a self-dependency makes the node permanently "unresolved" in a topological sort (it is either emitted last regardless of priority, or the sort trips its cycle handling), so the ranking and the resulting Now/Next split are wrong for such phases. The set should be `{owner[w] for w in waits if w in owner and owner[w] != pid}`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/kind_roadmap.py:_phase_before

chunk_findings.detail: The row emits `"ready": False` as a literal, even though the line directly above computes exactly that predicate (`any(r["status"] == "ready" for r in open_rows)`). Consequently every phase, including one with ready, unblocked tasks (the ones `lane_of` classifies as `"next"`), is reported as not ready. Any consumer that distinguishes ready phases — the Now-lane promotion described in the intent ("in flight plus the top N ready phases") or a readiness marker in the template — can never observe a ready phase; the value should be derived from the tasks (as `blocked_by` already does) rather than hardcoded.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/kind_roadmap.py:_phase_rows (row dict, `"ready": False`)

chunk_findings.detail: The change's stated intent is "Now = in flight plus the top N ready phases, Next = other ready, Later = waiting", but `split_lanes` puts the top N ready phases in the **Next** lane and never in **Now**: `now` is built only from phases whose lane is `"now"` (in-flight), while `nxt = ready[:max(next_n, 0)]` moves exactly the top-N ready phases into the second return value, and the remaining ready phases are pushed into `later` (marked `"ready": True`). Concretely, given phases already in order `[P1(ready), P2(ready), P3(waiting)]` and `next_n = 2`, `lane_of` yields lanes `ready, ready, later`, and `split_lanes` returns `now=[]`, `next=[P1, P2]`, `later=[P3]`. The rendered roadmap therefore has an empty "Now" section and shows the two actionable ready phases under "Next", i.e. the phases the plan says belong in Now (in-flight plus the top N ready) are reported in the wrong lane, and the "other ready" phases the plan puts in Next are instead shown in Later. (The module docstring at roadmap_calc.py:5 repeats the code's behaviour — "Now = work in flight, Next = the top N ready phases" — so the lane membership in the output contradicts the change's own stated intent.)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/roadmap_calc.py:68-79 (`split_lanes`)

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion is written without parentheses, so Python evaluates it as `(on and "P1" not in on) or (chain[0] in {"T2", "T3"})`. chunk_findings.detail:
`hide`, `next`, `tasks` and `show_hidden` are added to the global `EXPORT_TABLE_KEYS` and validated for *every* `[export.<doc>]` table, although the knob's own doc text scopes them to the roadmap ("the roadmap also takes hide …"). Two concrete consequences, both regressions relative to the documented rule “Unknown keys in an `[export.<doc>]` table are skipped with a warning”:

1. Misuse is silently accepted: with `[export.issues] tasks = 10` (or `hide = ["BL-"]`) the table now validates fine, `tasks` is never consumed by the issues exporter, and the user gets no warning that the key is meaningless there — whereas any other stale key still warns. The supplied `doc` argument is available but never used to scope the check, even though `_export_table_problem(doc, t)` is called once per table name.
2. A previously tolerated config now hard-fails: for `[export.changelog] next = "2.0"` (a key of another table that ddflow used to treat as unknown, warn and ignore), `_roadmap_keys_problem` returns `"[export.changelog].next must be an integer >= 0"`, which `_export_table_problem` propagates into the `tables` knob check and aborts config load/export — an existing checkout's configuration stops working because of a key that has nothing to do with the roadmap. Guarding the check with the document name (only `roadmap` gets these four keys, everything else keeps the warn-and-ignore path) avoids both effects.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/export.py:_roadmap_keys_problem (and EXPORT_TABLE_KEYS)

chunk_findings.detail: Every phase row is emitted with `ready` hardcoded to `False`, so the value is never derived from the phase's tasks. For the input "a phase whose only open task is in state `ready`" (e.g. one task with `status == "ready"`), `open_rows` contains a ready row, `RC.lane_of(open_rows, ...)` returns the ready lane, and the row is emitted as `"ready": False`. The same predicate is computed three lines above (`any(r["status"] == "ready" for r in open_rows)`, used to decide whether `blocked_by` is empty), so the row is internally inconsistent: a phase the module itself treats as unblocked/ready is reported as not ready. Any consumer that reads `phase.ready` — e.g. `RC.split_lanes` promoting "the top N ready phases" into Now or the template marking a Now phase as ready rather than in-flight — will see no ready phase at all, so the documented split "Now = in flight plus the top N ready phases, Next = other ready" degenerates to in-flight-only. The field should be computed from the open rows (and from whether the phase itself is in flight) rather than fixed to `False`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/kind_roadmap.py `_phase_rows` (`"ready": False`)

chunk_findings.detail: `cap_tasks` opens with `if cap <= 0 or len(rows) <= cap: return rows, 0`, so any cap that is zero (or negative) is treated as "no limit" and the full row list is returned together with `0` omitted. That contradicts both the function's own docstring ("At most ``cap`` open tasks") and the sibling convention in this file: `split_lanes` clamps with `max(next_n, 0)`, i.e. a `next`/`tasks` value of 0 means "none", not "unlimited". Concretely, with a config of `[export.roadmap] tasks = 0` and one phase holding 5 open tasks, `cap_tasks(rows, 0)` returns all 5 rows and `dropped == 0`, so the rendered Now/Next task list shows every task instead of nothing (and reports nothing as omitted). Without the `cap <= 0` guard the `ranked[:cap]` fall-through would already produce `[]` for `cap == 0`; the guard is only needed for negative values, where it should clamp to zero rather than disable the cap.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/roadmap_calc.py:84 (cap_tasks)

chunk_findings.detail: The test builds a log `g` that is supposed to have two release lines (`g.phase("P1", ...)`, `g.add("item.updated", "P1", {"line": "1.x"})`, `g.phase("P2", ...)`), but the assertions never query it: it asserts `data(road_log())["release_lines"] == []` (a different log that has no lines) and then tests the pure helper `RC.by_line([...])` on hand-written dicts. `g` is therefore dead fixture. The intended call `data(g)` would fail on such a regression.

chunk_findings.detail: The test name and the fixture claim to check that phases are ordered by dependency *then by priority* (the fixture sets priorities 90 / 10 / 50 and the log `g` is built for that), but the actual call is `RC.order(["A","B","C"], lambda i: {"B": ["A"]}.get(i, []), lambda i: (1, i))` — the third argument returns `(1, i)` for every phase, discarding the priorities entirely. The only assertion is `order.index("A") < order.index("B")`, i.e. the dependency edge. So an implementation of `RC.order` that ignores the priority key (or that the caller feeds the wrong priority) still passes; the "then priority" half of the topological-then-priority behavior described in the intent is never exercised, and the `g` fixture with its priorities is unused.

chunk_findings.detail: `owner` maps every task of a phase back to that phase (`owner[t.id] = pid`), and `before(pid)` unions the unmet deps of the phase *and of all its tasks* without ever excluding `pid` itself. The set should be `{owner[w] for w in waits if w in owner and owner[w] != pid}`.

chunk_findings.detail: Every phase row is emitted with `ready` hardcoded to `False`, so the value is never derived from the phase's tasks. For the input "a phase whose only open task is in state `ready`" (e.g. one task with `status == "ready"`), `open_rows` contains a ready row, `RC.lane_of(open_rows, ...)` returns the ready lane, and the row is emitted as `"ready": False`. The same predicate is computed three lines above (`any(r["status"] == "ready" for r in open_rows)`, used to decide whether `blocked_by` is empty), so the row is internally inconsistent: a phase the module itself treats as unblocked/ready is reported as not ready. Any consumer that reads `phase.ready` — e.g. `RC.split_lanes` promoting "the top N ready phases" into Now or the template marking a Now phase as ready rather than in-flight — will see no ready phase at all, so the documented split "Now = in flight plus the top N ready phases, Next = other ready" degenerates to in-flight-only. The field should be computed from the open rows (and from whether the phase itself is in flight) rather than fixed to `False`.

chunk_findings.detail: `cap_tasks` opens with `if cap <= 0 or len(rows) <= cap: return rows, 0`, so any cap that is zero (or negative) is treated as "no limit" and the full row list is returned together with `0` omitted. That contradicts both the function's own docstring ("At most ``cap`` open tasks") and the sibling convention in this file: `split_lanes` clamps with `max(next_n, 0)`, i.e. a `next`/`tasks` value of 0 means "none", not "unlimited". Concretely, with a config of `[export.roadmap] tasks = 0` and one phase holding 5 open tasks, `cap_tasks(rows, 0)` returns all 5 rows and `dropped == 0`, so the rendered Now/Next task list shows every task instead of nothing (and reports nothing as omitted). chunk_findings.detail: The witness test treats a path that runs *through the edge being tested* as proof that the edge is redundant, so an edge feeding into a dependency cycle is silently deleted and its source node is left with no edges at all. Concretely, with members `['a','b','i']`, `before('a') = []`, `before('b') = ['i']`, `before('i') = ['a','b']` (i.e. `i` waits on `a` and `b`, and `b`/`i` form a 2‑cycle): when processing `i`, `pre[i] = {'a','b'}`, and `below('b')` is computed as `{'i','a'}` because `pre[b] - {'b'} = {'i'}` recurses into `i`, which returns `a`. So `any('a' in below(o) for o in pre[i] if o != 'a')` is `True` and edge `('a','i')` is dropped. The only "longer path" `a → i → b → i` starts with the very edge under test, yet the final edge list is only `[('i','b'), ('b','i')]` — phase `a`, a genuine prerequisite of `i`, is rendered as an isolated node and the dependency is lost. The docstring on line 22 claims "A cycle's edges are kept as they are", and the test suite only covers a bare cycle, so this adjacent-edge case goes unnoticed. (The same root cause also lets `reach[i]` be cached as the truncated `{'a'}` on line 33 when reached under a non-empty `stack`, so the memo is order-dependent for cyclic input.)

chunk_findings.detail: The reduction removes an edge `(d, i)` whenever *any* other prerequisite `o` of `i` reaches `d` — but `below(o)` is computed on the graph that still contains the edge `(d, i)`, so in a cyclic input the justifying path can run back through `i`, and the edge is dropped without any alternative path to `i`. Concrete input: `ids = ["d", "i", "o"]`, `before("i") == ["d", "o"]`, `before("o") == ["i"]`, `before("d") == []`. Then `below(o)` evaluates to `{i} | below(i, {"o"}) == {i, d}` (`below(i, {"o"})` is `pre["i"] - {"o"} - {"i"} == {"d"}`), so for `i = "i"` and `d = "d"` the guard sees `d in below("o")` and appends no edge; the emitted edge list is `[("i","o"), ("o","i")]`, i.e. the phase `d` renders as an isolated node with no arrow to `i`, silently hiding the dependency “`i` waits on `d`”. The path used as justification (`o` depends on `i`, `i` depends on `d`, `i` depends on `o`) loops through `i` itself, so removing `(d,i)` does not preserve reachability — the docstring’s contract (“every edge a longer path already implies removed”, cycle edges kept) is violated for an edge that is *outside* the `i`↔`o` cycle. A correct reduction must establish the longer path without re-entering `i` (or without using the edge under test), not merely test `d in below(o)` on the unreduced graph. The same stack-truncated `reach` cache (`below(d, stack | {i})` memoized in the shared `reach` dict) is what makes the result depend on traversal/phase order for cyclic inputs.

chunk_findings.detail: The witness test treats a path that runs *through the edge being tested* as proof that the edge is redundant, so an edge feeding into a dependency cycle is silently deleted and its source node is left with no edges at all. Concretely, with members `['a','b','i']`, `before('a') = []`, `before('b') = ['i']`, `before('i') = ['a','b']` (i.e. `i` waits on `a` and `b`, and `b`/`i` form a 2‑cycle): when processing `i`, `pre[i] = {'a','b'}`, and `below('b')` is computed as `{'i','a'}` because `pre[b] - {'b'} = {'i'}` recurses into `i`, which returns `a`. So `any('a' in below(o) for o in pre[i] if o != 'a')` is `True` and edge `('a','i')` is dropped. The only "longer path" `a → i → b → i` starts with the very edge under test, yet the final edge list is only `[('i','b'), ('b','i')]` — phase `a`, a genuine prerequisite of `i`, is rendered as an isolated node and the dependency is lost. The docstring on line 22 claims "A cycle's edges are kept as they are", and the test suite only covers a bare cycle, so this adjacent-edge case goes unnoticed. (The same root cause also lets `reach[i]` be cached as the truncated `{'a'}` on line 33 when reached under a non-empty `stack`, so the memo is order-dependent for cyclic input.)

Both deletions are individually "witnessed" by the other edge's path (`a->b->i` and `a->i->b`), so `reduce_edges` returns `[('i','b'), ('b','i')]` and node `a` is left with no edges at all, even though `a` is a genuine prerequisite of both `b` and `i`. Reachability from `a` is lost in the rendered graph. The guard `not reaches(d, o, i)` only protects the case where the alternate path runs back *through the node being processed* (`i`); here the mutual justification runs through `b`, which the guard never inspects, so the earlier fix does not answer this input. chunk_findings.detail: The reduction removes an edge `(d, i)` whenever *any* other prerequisite `o` of `i` reaches `d` — but `below(o)` is computed on the graph that still contains the edge `(d, i)`, so in a cyclic input the justifying path can run back through `i`, and the edge is dropped without any alternative path to `i`. Concrete input: `ids = ["d", "i", "o"]`, `before("i") == ["d", "o"]`, `before("o") == ["i"]`, `before("d") == []`. Then `below(o)` evaluates to `{i} | below(i, {"o"}) == {i, d}` (`below(i, {"o"})` is `pre["i"] - {"o"} - {"i"} == {"d"}`), so for `i = "i"` and `d = "d"` the guard sees `d in below("o")` and appends no edge; the emitted edge list is `[("i","o"), ("o","i")]`, i.e. the phase `d` renders as an isolated node with no arrow to `i`, silently hiding the dependency “`i` waits on `d`”. The path used as justification (`o` depends on `i`, `i` depends on `d`, `i` depends on `o`) loops through `i` itself, so removing `(d,i)` does not preserve reachability — the docstring’s contract (“every edge a longer path already implies removed”, cycle edges kept) is violated for an edge that is *outside* the `i`↔`o` cycle. A correct reduction must establish the longer path without re-entering `i` (or without using the edge under test), not merely test `d in below(o)` on the unreduced graph. The same stack-truncated `reach` cache (`below(d, stack | {i})` memoized in the shared `reach` dict) is what makes the result depend on traversal/phase order for cyclic inputs.
